hops.afterHeading: The graft: whose cells built the second back?
hops.title: Ethel Browne's 1909 Hydra graft
hops.text: Fifteen years before Spemann and Mangold's paper, Columbia graduate student Ethel Browne published a 1909 study of Hydra, a freshwater polyp with tentacles around its mouth. Using the same colour trick in the winters of 1906–1908, she made a green Hydra colourless and grafted one pale tentacle with a bit of tissue at its base onto a green host of the same species. Green host body-wall cells were, in her words, changed over to build a second head, while the pale donor tentacle stayed in the new ring. Spemann never cited the study in his papers. In 1991, Howard Lenhoff published an account of its place in organizer history.

sources.citation: Thomann & Batut (2026), eLife 15:e110644 (citing Browne 1909, J. Exp. Zool. 7:1-23)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A green Hydra polyp growing a second green head with green tentacles and one pale tentacle on its side, beside a colourless Hydra in a clear glass dish.
image.caption: Grafting a pale tentacle with tissue from its base made green host cells build a second Hydra head.

hops.title: Mutant chicken embryos that form alligator-like tooth buds
hops.text: The ancestors of modern birds lost mineralized teeth, and for years one explanation was that the tissue beneath the embryonic mouth lining had lost its ability to help form them. In one graft study, chick mouth lining could still prompt mouse-derived jaw cells to start forming tooth structures. Then, in 2006, Matthew Harris and colleagues reported that embryos of a chicken mutant called talpid2 form early tooth rudiments resembling the first ones in alligator embryos. Harris's group proposed that birds lost teeth when a signalling centre in the mouth lining shifted out of alignment with the jaw tissue that could still respond and start forming teeth.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A curious red hen on a wooden fence post looking down at a green alligator beside a mound of leaves and grasses near the water.
image.caption: A mutant chicken embryo forms tooth buds resembling the first rudimentary ones in an alligator embryo.

hops.afterHeading: More than one induction: the organizer builds an axis
hops.title: What lithium does to a frog embryo's organizer
hops.text: Lithium, one of the most effective drugs for bipolar disorder, has a strange second career in embryology. In 1986, and in more detail in 1988, researchers briefly bathed cleavage-stage Xenopus embryos in lithium. The embryos grew a ring-shaped eye, a greatly enlarged notochord and a ring-shaped beating heart. Grafts cut from any point around the equator rescued dorsal structures in embryos that lacked them: lithium had turned the whole equator into organizer. In 1996, Peter Klein and Douglas Melton showed that lithium inhibits an enzyme that helps break down β-catenin. In a separate study, researchers found more β-catenin in the nuclei of lithium-treated embryos.

sources.citation: Kao & Elinson (1988), Developmental Biology 127(1):64-77 (citing Kao, Masui & Elinson 1986, Nature 322:371-373)
Schneider et al. (1996), Mechanisms of Development 57(2):191-198

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An African clawed frog in a glass bowl beside a small porcelain dish of white salt crystals and a dish of translucent frog eggs.
image.caption: Lithium inhibits an enzyme helping break down β-catenin; early-cleavage exposure can extend organizer activity around a Xenopus embryo's whole equator.
